title: Decomposition-Based QAOA for Maximum Coverage Location Problem in Satellite Constellation Design
authors: Divya Sisodiya, Amiratabak Bahengam, Hang Woon Lee, Hao Chen
abstract: An increase in earth observation missions has increased the demand of efficient design and optimization of satellite constellations. Maximizing coverage of the target while effectively utilizing the limited orbital resources is one of the critical design challenges for complex combinatorial optimization problems. The maximal covering location problem (MCLP), serves as a base for orbital coverage modeling, is NP-hard and computationally intractable for large-constellation instances. Using heuristics, metaheuristics, and mixed-integer linear programming, classical solvers have achieved optimal or near-optimal results, yet their scalability is limited as the problem size increases. Quantum computing advancements, including the quantum approximate optimization algorithms, offer a potential solution to NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems. Current quantum hardware limitations, such as low qubit counts and circuit depth, restrict solutions for small-scale instance problems. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a scalable quantum optimization framework for MCLP in satellite constellation design. A decomposition-based quantum methodology is proposed, in which large MCLP instances are partitioned into subgraphs by classical decomposition, optimized independently via quantum optimization circuits, and combined using quantum reconstruction strategies. Computational results across different constellation sizes reveal better scalability in less time while maintaining competitive coverage performance compared to classical solvers.
summary: This paper proposes a novel, scalable quantum approach using decomposition methods to solve the computationally hard Maximal Covering Location Problem (MCLP) for satellite constellation design. By partitioning the large problem into smaller subproblems solved via QAOA and then merging the results, the authors overcome the limitations of current quantum hardware on massive instances. The framework shows promise by maintaining high coverage performance while achieving better scalability than classical or standard quantum methods.
main_problem: The core problem is optimizing satellite constellation design by solving the NP-hard Maximal Covering Location Problem (MCLP) to maximize ground coverage.
main_result: A decomposition-based QAOA framework demonstrates better scalability and competitive coverage performance for large MCLP instances compared to standard quantum or classical solvers.
method: The method uses spectral bisection on a co-observation graph to partition the large MCLP into smaller subproblems, which are then solved independently using QAOA circuits before being combined via quantum reconstruction strategies (GSR/QSR).
model_or_system: The system is an Earth observation satellite constellation modeled by orbital slots and ground targets. The problem is formulated as an Ising Hamiltonian derived from the MCLP constraints, which are then mapped onto a QUBO representation.
key_observables: Coverage Ratio (Approximation ratio $ho$), Runtime ($T$), and Optimality Gap.
important_parameters: Number of orbital slots ($J$), number of satellites ($N$), maximum subgraph size ($q_{	ext{max}}$), and circuit depth ($p$).
main_assumptions: The approach assumes that decomposing the problem into smaller, hardware-tractable subproblems mitigates the exponential scaling issues faced by standard QAOA on large instances. The use of GSR is shown to outperform QSR.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the decomposition framework flow; Figure 12 compares approximation ratios ($ho$) between IBM hardware and OpenQAOA simulator, showing noise effects; Table VIII summarizes mean runtimes with 95% Confidence Intervals for various visibility matrix instances.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes MCLP as an intractable problem. It then introduces the decomposition-based QAOA framework, detailing graph construction via spectral bisection and solving subproblems using QAOA. Finally, it compares the performance of different merging strategies (GSR vs QSR) on both simulated and actual quantum hardware.
why_interesting: While focused on optimization rather than fundamental physics, the methodology—applying divide-and-conquer techniques to map a complex combinatorial problem onto NISQ devices—is highly relevant for developing scalable quantum algorithms for physical simulations in condensed matter or AMO contexts.
